title: Muscles of the Lower Limb
introduction: The musculature of the lower limb is organized regionally across the gluteal region, posterior thigh, anterior, lateral, and posterior compartments of the leg, and the dorsal and plantar aspects of the foot[cite: 100]. Together, these compartments stabilize the hip, drive gait through hip extension and knee flexion, control ankle and subtalar movements, and support the digits and arches of the foot[cite: 100].
learningOutcomes: 5.1 Describe the boundaries, pelvic communications, superficial and deep muscle layers, bursae, and bursitis syndromes of the gluteal region[cite: 100].
5.2 State the four criteria defining a hamstring muscle and compare the attachments, innervation, and clinical injuries of the posterior thigh muscles[cite: 100].
5.3 Differentiate the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg by their constituent muscles, attachments, innervation, blood supply, and actions[cite: 100].
5.4 Outline the superficial and deep muscle layers of the posterior compartment of the leg, including the knee-unlocking role of the popliteus[cite: 100].
5.5 Classify the dorsal foot muscles and the four plantar layers of the foot, and summarize key clinical conditions of the leg and foot[cite: 100].

content.heading: Gluteal Region: Boundaries, Layers, and Bursae
content.body: Although physically part of the trunk, the gluteal region (buttock) is functionally part of the lower limb and is demarcated anteriorly from the trunk at the inguinal ligament[cite: 100]. It lies posterior to the pelvis and inferior to the iliac crests, bounded superomedially by the sacrum, medially by the natal (intergluteal) cleft, inferiorly by the gluteal sulcus, and laterally by a line joining the anterior superior iliac spine to the front of the greater trochanter[cite: 100]. It communicates with the pelvic cavity via the greater sciatic foramen, with the ischiorectal fossa via the lesser sciatic foramen, and is continuous inferiorly with the posterior thigh compartment[cite: 100]. Its muscles are arranged in two layers: the superficial layer (gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae), which mainly extend, abduct, and medially rotate the thigh; and the deep layer of short lateral rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli, and quadratus femoris), covered by the inferior half of gluteus maximus, which laterally rotate the thigh and stabilize the hip joint[cite: 100]. Three synovial gluteal bursae reduce friction: the trochanteric bursa (between gluteus maximus and the greater trochanter), the gluteofemoral bursa (between the gluteus maximus tendon and the origin of vastus lateralis), and the ischial bursa (between gluteus maximus and the lower medial ischial tuberosity)[cite: 100]. Friction over these sacs causes ischial bursitis (pain increasing with gluteus maximus movement) or trochanteric bursitis (from repetitive stair climbing with heavy loads or steeply inclined treadmill running)[cite: 100].

content.heading: Posterior Thigh Region (Hamstrings)
content.body: The posterior compartment of the thigh contains four muscles, three of which are true hamstrings: the long head of biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus[cite: 100]. To qualify as a hamstring, a muscle must originate from the ischial tuberosity, insert into the tibia or fibula, be innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, and act as both a hip extensor and knee flexor[cite: 100]. Semitendinosus inserts into the medial surface of the superior tibia, semimembranosus inserts into the posterior medial tibial condyle (with a reflected attachment forming the oblique popliteal ligament), and both extend the thigh, flex the leg, and medially rotate the flexed knee[cite: 100]. Biceps femoris inserts onto the lateral head of the fibula (split by the fibular collateral ligament) and laterally rotates the flexed knee; however, its short head arises from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur and is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2), so it fails the hamstring criteria[cite: 100]. Because no major artery runs down the posterior thigh, these muscles are supplied by perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery[cite: 100]. Clinically, runners are prone to pulled hamstrings (tearing at the ischial tuberosity), and forcible hip flexion with an extended knee can cause avulsion of the ischial tuberosity at the proximal attachment of biceps femoris and semitendinosus[cite: 100].

content.heading: Anterior and Lateral Compartments of the Leg
content.body: The anterior compartment of the leg primarily dorsiflexes the foot, is supplied by the anterior tibial artery, and is innervated by the deep fibular nerve[cite: 100]. It contains four muscles: tibialis anterior (most medial and superficial; originates from lateral tibial condyle and superior two-thirds of tibia to insert on the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal; dorsiflexes and inverts the foot), extensor digitorum longus (most lateral; from lateral tibial condyle, upper three-quarters of anterior fibula, and interosseous membrane to middle and distal phalanges of the lateral four toes; extends toes 2 to 5 and dorsiflexes), extensor hallucis longus (deep to both; from middle anteromedial fibula and interosseous membrane to distal phalanx of the great toe; extends the great toe), and fibularis tertius (distal extension of extensor digitorum longus; from inferior third of anterior fibula to dorsum of 5th metatarsal base; dorsiflexes and everts the foot)[cite: 100]. The lateral compartment everts the foot at the subtalar joint, is innervated by the superficial fibular nerve, and contains two muscles: fibularis longus (superficial and larger; from head and upper two-thirds of lateral fibula to medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; plantarflexes and everts) and fibularis brevis (shorter and deeper; from inferior two-thirds of lateral fibula to dorsal base of 5th metatarsal; everts and weakly plantarflexes)[cite: 100].

content.heading: Posterior Compartment of the Leg (Superficial and Deep Layers)
content.body: The posterior compartment of the leg plantarflexes the foot and is innervated by the tibial nerve[cite: 100]. Its superficial layer comprises three muscles: gastrocnemius (most superficial, forming the calf bulk via lateral and medial femoral condyle heads; converges with soleus into the calcaneal/Achilles tendon to plantarflex the ankle and flex the knee), soleus (flat and deep to gastrocnemius; arises from the tibial soleal line, medial tibia, and upper posterior fibula to insert via the Achilles tendon; plantarflexes the ankle), and plantaris (short fusiform belly and long tendon from the lateral supracondylar line and oblique popliteal ligament to the posterior calcaneus; flexes the knee and assists plantarflexion)[cite: 100]. Its deep layer contains four muscles: popliteus (thin triangular muscle forming the inferior floor of the popliteal fossa from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus to the posterior tibia above the soleal line; supplied by the popliteal artery; laterally rotates the femur on the tibia to unlock the knee for flexion), flexor digitorum longus (medial; from posterior tibia below soleal line to plantar distal phalanges II to V; flexes lateral four toes, plantarflexes, and inverts), flexor hallucis longus (unipennate, fibular side; from inferior two-thirds of posterior fibula to distal phalanx of great toe; flexes all joints of the great toe), and tibialis posterior (between FDL and FHL; passes behind the medial malleolus to attach to the navicular tuberosity, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali, and bases of metatarsals 2 to 4; plantarflexes and inverts the foot)[cite: 100].

content.heading: Dorsal Aspect and Plantar Layers 1 and 2 of the Foot
content.body: The dorsal aspect of the foot contains two intrinsic extensors innervated by the deep fibular nerve: extensor digitorum brevis (arises from the superolateral calcaneus and inferior extensor retinaculum, divides into three slips to the long extensor tendons of toes 2 to 4, supplied by the fibular and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis arteries) and extensor hallucis brevis (from the superolateral calcaneus to the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, assisting extension at the metatarsophalangeal joint)[cite: 100]. The plantar aspect (sole) is organized into four layers[cite: 100]. Layer 1 contains abductor hallucis (medial; calcaneal tuberosity to medial proximal phalanx of great toe; medial plantar nerve S2-S3; abducts and flexes great toe), flexor digitorum brevis (central; calcaneus and plantar aponeurosis to middle phalanges of lateral four toes; medial plantar nerve; flexes lateral four digits), and abductor digiti minimi (lateral; calcaneal tuberosity to lateral proximal phalanx of 5th digit; lateral plantar nerve; abducts and flexes little toe)[cite: 100]. Layer 2 contains quadratus plantae or flexor accessorius (calcaneus to posterolateral border of FDL tendon; lateral plantar nerve and artery; assists FDL in flexing lateral four digits) and four lumbricals (from FDL tendons to medial extensor hoods of toes 2 to 5; flex proximal phalanges and extend middle and distal phalanges; the 1st lumbrical is supplied by the medial plantar nerve, while the lateral three are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve)[cite: 100].

content.heading: Plantar Layers 3 and 4 of the Foot
content.body: Layer 3 of the sole comprises three short muscles acting on the first and fifth digits[cite: 100]. Flexor hallucis brevis arises from the plantar cuboid and lateral cuneiform to insert onto both sides of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, supplied by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3) and medial plantar artery to flex the proximal phalanx[cite: 100]. Adductor hallucis has two heads—a transverse head (from plantar ligaments of the 3rd to 5th metatarsophalangeal joints) and an oblique head (from plantar bases of the 2nd to 4th metatarsals)—inserting onto the lateral base of the great toe proximal phalanx and supplied by the deep part of the lateral plantar nerve to adduct the great toe[cite: 100]. Flexor digiti minimi brevis runs from the base of the 5th metatarsal to the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th digit, supplied by the superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve to flex the little toe[cite: 100]. Layer 4 contains the interossei, all innervated by the lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3): 3 plantar interossei (from medial sides of metatarsals 3 to 5 to extensor hoods and proximal phalanges of digits 3 to 5; adduct toes 3 to 5) and 4 dorsal interossei (from adjacent sides of metatarsals 1 to 5 to the medial proximal phalanx of toe 2 and lateral proximal phalanges of toes 2 to 4; abduct toes 2 to 4 away from the 2nd toe reference axis)[cite: 100].

content.heading: Applied Anatomy of the Leg and Foot
content.body: Common leg injuries include Achilles tendonitis (inflammation of the calcaneal tendon formed by gastrocnemius and soleus), shin splints or medial tibial stress syndrome (overuse or improper training affecting the tibialis anterior muscles), and gastrocnemius strain or 'tennis leg' (injury to the calf presenting with tenderness on palpation of the medial belly or musculotendinous junction)[cite: 100]. Key clinical conditions of the foot include plantar fasciitis (inflammation of the thick plantar fascia connecting the calcaneus to the toes), medial plantar nerve entrapment (compression of the medial plantar nerve), tarsal tunnel syndrome (compression of the tibial nerve), and contusion (bruising or damage) of extensor digitorum brevis[cite: 100].

inTextQuestions.question: Why is the short head of biceps femoris not classified as a true hamstring muscle?
inTextQuestions.answer: It fails the hamstring criteria because it arises from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur (not the ischial tuberosity) and is innervated by the common fibular division (not the tibial division) of the sciatic nerve[cite: 100].

inTextQuestions.question: Which muscle unlocks the extended knee joint so that knee flexion can begin, and how does it do so?
inTextQuestions.answer: The popliteus muscle laterally rotates the femur on the tibia to unlock the knee, allowing the knee to flex[cite: 100].

inTextQuestions.question: Which nerve innervates the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg, and what is their primary shared action?
inTextQuestions.answer: The superficial fibular nerve innervates fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, whose primary action is eversion of the foot at the subtalar joint (with plantarflexion)[cite: 100].

inTextQuestions.question: Which muscles of the sole of the foot are innervated by the medial plantar nerve?
inTextQuestions.answer: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, the first (medial) lumbrical, and flexor hallucis brevis[cite: 100].

saqs.question: List the four criteria a posterior thigh muscle must meet to be classified as a hamstring, and name the three true hamstring muscles.
saqs.answer: The four criteria are: (1) origin from the ischial tuberosity, (2) insertion into either the tibia or fibula, (3) nerve supply by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, and (4) action as an extensor of the hip joint and flexor of the knee joint[cite: 100]. The three true hamstrings are the long head of biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus[cite: 100].

saqs.question: Identify the three gluteal bursae, state the anatomical location of each, and explain what triggers trochanteric bursitis.
saqs.answer: The trochanteric bursa lies between gluteus maximus and the greater trochanter; the gluteofemoral bursa lies between the gluteus maximus tendon and the origin of vastus lateralis; and the ischial bursa lies between gluteus maximus and the lower medial ischial tuberosity[cite: 100]. Trochanteric bursitis results from repetitive actions such as climbing stairs carrying heavy objects or running on a steeply elevated treadmill, which move the superior tendinous fibers of gluteus maximus repeatedly over the bursa[cite: 100].

saqs.question: Name the four muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg and state their common nerve supply, blood supply, and primary compartment action.
saqs.answer: The four muscles are tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius[cite: 100]. They are innervated by the deep fibular nerve, supplied by the anterior tibial artery, and primarily perform dorsiflexion of the foot (along with toe extension, inversion by tibialis anterior, and eversion by fibularis tertius)[cite: 100].

saqs.question: Compare the plantar interossei and dorsal interossei of the fourth plantar layer in terms of count, attachments, action, and innervation.
saqs.answer: There are 3 plantar interossei originating from the medial sides of metatarsals 3 to 5 and inserting into the extensor hoods and proximal phalanges of digits 3 to 5 to adduct toes 3 to 5[cite: 100]. There are 4 dorsal interossei originating from adjacent sides of metatarsals 1 to 5 and inserting into the medial side of the 2nd toe and lateral sides of toes 2 to 4 to abduct toes 2 to 4 away from the 2nd toe axis[cite: 100]. Both groups are innervated by the lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3)[cite: 100].

saqs.question: Define Achilles tendonitis, shin splints, gastrocnemius strain (tennis leg), plantar fasciitis, and tarsal tunnel syndrome.
saqs.answer: Achilles tendonitis is inflammation of the Achilles tendon formed by gastrocnemius and soleus[cite: 100]; shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) is an overuse injury affecting the tibialis anterior muscles[cite: 100]; gastrocnemius strain (tennis leg) is a calf muscle injury presenting with pain on palpating the medial belly or musculotendinous junction[cite: 100]; plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the thick plantar fascia connecting the calcaneus to the toes[cite: 100]; and tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the tibial nerve[cite: 100].
